name: Imran
definition: Imran is a composite portrait of a dal mill floor supervisor in Yelburga town, Koppal district, Kalyana Karnataka region. He represents Muslim working men in the tur-dal processing economy that makes Koppal and neighbouring Kalaburagi districts central to India's pigeon-pea trade.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Imran supervises the sorting and bagging lines at a medium-sized dal mill on the edge of Yelburga town, where tur-dal brought from APMC yards across Koppal and Kalaburagi is cleaned, split and graded. He arrives at five in the morning during peak milling season—October through February—when lorries queue outside and the machines run two shifts. His day is spent checking moisture meters, managing the women who hand-sort the split dal, and keeping the packaging line moving to meet wholesale orders bound for Bengaluru and the coast. The mill pays him a monthly salary of around fourteen thousand rupees, with a small seasonal bonus if tonnage targets are met. Income is steady compared to farming, but the work is exhausting and the air thick with dal dust. The mill owner is a Lingayat trader who runs three units across the district; Imran has worked for him for sixteen years, rising from the bagging crew. During the lean months—June to September—milling slows and his hours are cut, so the household tightens its budget. His wife stitches blouses at home for a neighbourhood tailor, adding three to four thousand rupees a month. They live in a rented two-room house near the old bus stand, within walking distance of the mill and the town mosque.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Imran's household includes his wife Farhana, their three children—two daughters aged seventeen and fourteen, and a son aged ten—and his widowed mother, who is in her late sixties. His father, a bullock-cart driver, died eight years ago, and his mother now lives with them, spending her days in prayer and helping with the younger children. Farhana manages the home, cooks, and does piecework tailoring when orders come in; she attended school only until Class 5. The older daughter completed her SSLC last year at the government high school in Yelburga and now stays at home, helping her mother and waiting while the family considers whether to let her continue to PUC or arrange her marriage. The younger daughter is in Class 9 at the same school. The son is in Class 5 at the Urdu-medium primary school attached to the town mosque. Imran's two brothers live in Koppal town; one drives an auto-rickshaw and the other works as a shop assistant. The brothers gather for Eid and weddings but do not share household expenses. Gender roles are clear: Farhana handles all domestic work and childcare, Imran earns and manages money, and his mother's authority in religious and family matters is respected.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Imran himself studied up to Class 7 at the Urdu-medium school in Yelburga before leaving to work in the dal mills as a teenager; his family needed the income and saw no route forward in further schooling. He can read Urdu and enough Kannada to manage mill paperwork. His older daughter passed her SSLC in the Kannada-medium government high school with a second-class mark; the family is proud but unsure whether sending her to PUC college in Yelburga is worth the cost and risk, given that girls from their neighbourhood rarely continue past SSLC and marriage is expected. The younger daughter is a good student, and Imran wants her to finish at least SSLC. His son attends the Urdu-medium primary school because Imran and Farhana wanted him to learn to read the Quran properly; they plan to shift him to Kannada-medium for high school so he can compete for government jobs under the 371(J) quota if his marks are strong. School fees are low—around five hundred rupees a year for each child in government schools—but books, uniforms, and the PUC college fee would add up. Imran hopes his son will study further, perhaps get a diploma or a government job, and not spend his life breathing dal dust.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Imran has a persistent cough—common among dal-mill workers—from years of inhaling grain dust; he has never been formally diagnosed but knows it worsens in peak season. The family uses the government taluk hospital in Yelburga for fevers and minor illnesses; they wait hours but pay little. His mother has joint pain and high blood pressure; she takes tablets from the hospital and sees a local Unani hakim for herbal remedies. Farhana had a difficult delivery with their youngest child and was referred to the district hospital in Koppal town; the 108 ambulance took her, and she recovered, but the episode left the family in debt for two years. The children are vaccinated and generally healthy. Imran worries about his cough and what will happen if he cannot work, but he has no health insurance—only an Ayushman Bharat card that the family has never used. The drinking water in their neighbourhood comes from a borewell; they boil it after hearing of fluoride problems in some Koppal villages. No one in the household smokes, but Imran chews gutka occasionally during long shifts, a habit he knows he should stop. The older daughter's health and marriage prospects weigh on Farhana's mind.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Imran's family belongs to Yelburga's Muslim community, which makes up a significant share of the town's population and is part of the Dakhni Urdu-speaking network across Kalyana Karnataka. They pray five times a day, and Imran attends Friday prayers at the town mosque whenever his mill shift allows. Farhana observes purdah loosely—she covers her head in public but moves freely within the neighbourhood. Ramzan and Eid are the most important festivals; the family fasts, prepares biryani and sheer khurma, and visits relatives in Koppal town. Imran's mother insists on reading the Quran daily and teaching the grandson. The family has never visited the Khwaja Bande Nawaz Dargah in Kalaburagi, though they know of its importance and hope to go someday. Social ties are dense within the Muslim neighbourhood—neighbours help each other with loans, childcare, and wedding expenses. Imran is not active in any political organisation but feels the community's interests are often ignored. Caste is not a category he uses within the Muslim fold, but he is acutely aware of the economic distance between his mill-supervisor job and the Lingayat and Vokkaliga dal traders who own the mills and the land.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He has never approached the taluk office or a local MLA for help. The family receives ten kilograms of rice per month under Anna Bhagya, which makes a real difference to the household budget. Farhana uses the Shakti free-bus scheme to visit her mother in a nearby village, a trip she could not have afforded regularly before. Imran knows about Article 371(J) and the local-recruitment quota but does not understand the details; he hopes it will help his son get a government job someday if he studies well. He has heard of the Kalyana Karnataka Regional Development Board but does not know what it has built in Yelburga. The town's streets are poorly maintained, and the neighbourhood's drainage is a mess during the monsoon. Imran blames local contractors and officials for siphoning funds but does not expect anything to change. The dal mill is not registered under any labour welfare scheme, and he has no provident fund or pension. Politics feels distant—something decided by powerful people in Bengaluru and Koppal town.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Imran is proud of his steady job and his climb from mill labourer to supervisor, and he takes satisfaction in providing for his family without depending on anyone. But he worries constantly—about his cough and his ability to keep working, about his older daughter's future and whether they will find a decent match without a heavy dowry, about his son's education and whether the boy will have better opportunities than he did. He resents the fact that decades of dal-milling wealth have enriched a handful of trader families while workers like him remain trapped in rented houses, and he is frustrated that Koppal's schools and hospital lag so far behind what he hears about Bengaluru. He sees the 371(J) quota as a rare chance for his son but doubts it will amount to much if the boy cannot afford coaching or if the system is rigged by people with connections. Imran does not blame his community or religion for the family's struggles; he blames a lack of opportunity, unequal access to education, and an indifferent government. He wants his children to study, his daughters to marry into secure families, and his son to escape the dal dust. He believes in hard work, prayer, and looking after one's own family, but he has no faith that the state or the district administration will ever do much for people like him.
